bill.name: Judicial Ethics Enforcement Act of 2025 (H.R. 1811)
bill.status: Introduced in House · Stansbury · referred to House Judiciary on March 3, 2025
bill.analyzed: Full introduced-in-House bill (7 pages; §§1–2), with §2 adding proposed 28 U.S.C. §§1021–1026.

sourceLimits: The supplied 6,804-byte, 1,114-word raw source contains all substantive clauses of the introduced-in-House bill but is flattened into one line, has no page boundaries or metadata sidecar, and omits the standard enacting clause visible in the matching official PDF. That PDF establishes the seven-page count, and the official Congress.gov record establishes the introduced status. The bill incorporates or invokes external materials, including 28 U.S.C. chapter 16 and §§352(c) and 354(b), the title 5 competitive-service provisions, title 5 chapter 51 and subchapter III of chapter 53, 5 U.S.C. §§3109 and 5315, and the Code of Conduct for Justices of the Supreme Court, without reproducing them; this extraction does not infer requirements beyond the bill's descriptions and express cross-references. The text contains no findings or purpose section, so its goals are restrained inferences from the duties, powers, limits, and protection it would enact. It sets no express effective or office-start date, appointment deadline, acting-officer mechanism, funding amount, staffing level, first-report deadline, report format, public-release requirement, or quantitative misconduct, waste, fraud, abuse, retaliation, or institutional-integrity target. Section 1024(a)(7) also literally begins “the extent” rather than “to the extent,” a grammatical defect in the appropriation-conditioned contracting clause. Appointment and removal events are discrete governance records, while annual, prompt, sensitive, and criminal-referral reports may be nonpublic and need not contain standardized fields. Counts of allegations, investigations, referrals, or civil actions would also be directionally ambiguous: an increase could reflect more misconduct or retaliation, greater reporting, or greater enforcement capacity. Neither the supplied source nor the local Thesis docket identifies a recurring official public series that directly measures implementation or outcomes. This extraction therefore identifies zero currently automatable public-series metrics and contains no series hints, stance matrices, or mechanically resolvable empirical conditionals; it does not treat office creation or report transmission as proof that misconduct, waste, fraud, abuse, or retaliation would fall.

provisions.title: Section 2 — Office, jurisdiction, powers, limits, and reports
provisions.heading: 1. Proposed 28 U.S.C. §§1021–1025: establish and equip a judicial-branch Inspector General
provisions.quote: “There is established for the judicial branch of the Government the Office of Inspector General for the Judicial Branch” … “conduct investigations of alleged violations of the Code of Conduct for Justices of the Supreme Court of the United States” … “make an annual report to the Chief Justice and to Congress relating to the activities of the Office”.
provisions.context: Section 1 supplies only the short title. Section 2(a) would add chapter 60 to part III of title 28. Proposed §1021 establishes the Office. Section 1022 places appointment, unlimited reappointment, and removal with the Chief Justice: appointment follows consultation with the four named congressional leaders, each term lasts four years, and removal requires the Chief Justice to communicate reasons to both Houses; the bill states no congressional-consent requirement and no cause standard for removal. Sections 1023 and 1024 direct investigations of alleged non-Supreme-Court misconduct under chapter 16 and alleged Supreme Court Code violations or other Supreme Court misconduct, require the Office to conduct and supervise audits and investigations, direct prevention and detection of waste, fraud, and abuse, and authorize recommendations for legal or regulatory change. They authorize information or assistance from governmental and other entities—expressly including the Judicial Conference, circuit judicial councils, Administrative Office of the United States Courts, and United States Sentencing Commission—subpoenas enforceable by civil action, oaths, hiring subject to the cited competitive-service, classification, and General Schedule pay provisions, expert services capped at the daily equivalent of Executive Schedule level IV, and appropriation-conditioned contracting. A §1023(1) investigation cannot begin until denial of a §352(c) petition for review or referral or certification under §354(b); the text does not state a parallel gate for the separate Supreme Court authority in §1023(2). The Inspector General cannot review matters directly related to the merits of a decision or procedural ruling and cannot punish or discipline a judge, justice, or court. Section 1025 requires annual and prompt reports to the Chief Justice and Congress and expeditious notice to the Attorney General whenever the Inspector General has reasonable grounds to believe there has been a violation of Federal criminal law; Congress may receive sensitive reports in closed session. Section 2(b) makes only the conforming chapter-table amendment. The bill supplies no express effective date, implementation schedule, or public-reporting requirement.
goals: Create a dedicated Inspector General office for the judicial branch under a leader appointed by the Chief Justice after consultation with the Senate majority and minority leaders and the House Speaker and minority leader.
Investigate alleged non-Supreme-Court misconduct under chapter 16, alleged violations of the Supreme Court's Code of Conduct, and other alleged Supreme Court misconduct.
Conduct audits, prevent and detect waste, fraud, and abuse, and recommend changes to laws or regulations governing the judicial branch.

Report Office activities and matters that may require action to the Chief Justice and Congress, notify the Attorney General when the statutory reasonable-grounds threshold for a Federal criminal-law violation is met, and exclude merits or procedural-ruling review and punishment or discipline of judges, justices, or courts from the Inspector General's authority.

effects.mechanism: Office creation without a stand-up clock
effects.text: Enactment would establish the Office and an Inspector General serving a four-year term in title 28, but the text sets no appointment deadline, acting-officer rule, initial staffing target, or date by which the Office must begin operations.

effects.mechanism: Chief Justice appointment and removal authority with congressional notice
effects.text: The Chief Justice would appoint the Inspector General after consultation, could reappoint the Inspector General for unlimited additional terms, and could remove the Inspector General without a stated cause standard. Communicating removal reasons to Congress adds notice but does not require congressional approval.

effects.mechanism: Separate non-Supreme-Court and Supreme Court oversight routes
effects.text: The Inspector General could not commence a §1023(1) investigation into non-Supreme-Court chapter 16 misconduct until denial of a §352(c) petition for review or referral or certification under §354(b). The text states no parallel commencement gate for alleged Supreme Court Code violations or other alleged Supreme Court misconduct under §1023(2).

Broad information-access, subpoena, oath, hiring, and service authorities could increase investigative capacity. Hiring would be subject to the cited competitive-service, classification, and General Schedule pay rules, and §3109 services could not exceed the daily equivalent of Executive Schedule level IV. A resisted subpoena would require civil enforcement, and the text does not specify how that process interacts with privilege, sealed records, or other confidentiality claims.

The Office could investigate, audit, report, notify the Attorney General when it has reasonable grounds to believe Federal criminal law was violated, and recommend changes, but it could not review adjudicative merits or punish or discipline judges, justices, or courts. Any punishment or discipline of a judge, justice, or court—and any legislative or prosecutorial consequence—would therefore depend on another actor; the bill grants the Inspector General no express disciplinary authority over other personnel.

Annual and prompt reports would create official transmissions to the Chief Justice and Congress, while the Inspector General would notify the Attorney General whenever the statutory reasonable-grounds threshold for a Federal criminal-law violation was met. The bill does not require public release or standardized contents, and sensitive reports may be received in closed session.

barriers.actor: Chief Justice and the new Office
barriers.text: The Chief Justice would have to appoint the Inspector General, and the new leadership would have to build an operating office without an appointment deadline, acting-officer mechanism, transition rule, first-report date, or other implementation schedule.

The bill provides no appropriation or funding level. It permits staffing and expert services, while its contracting clause is expressly limited by advance appropriations and contains the literal grammatical omission “the extent” where “to the extent” appears necessary.

They would have to determine when the chapter 16 predicates are satisfied and distinguish investigable misconduct from matters directly related to decisional merits or procedural rulings, including cases in which conduct and case handling overlap.

barriers.actor: Records holders, witnesses, and enforcing courts
barriers.text: The Office's work could depend on access to sensitive judicial information and civil enforcement of resisted subpoenas, while the text supplies no special procedure for privilege, sealed material, confidentiality disputes, venue, or enforcement timing.

barriers.actor: Chief Justice, Congress, Attorney General, and public evaluators
barriers.text: Reports and recommendations have no automatic remedy or adoption rule. Because publication and standardized activity fields are not required, outsiders may be unable to verify transmissions, referrals, investigative volume, dispositions, or follow-through.

provisions.title: Section 2 — Whistleblower protection and civil action
provisions.heading: 2. Proposed 28 U.S.C. §1026: protect employees whose lawful disclosures or investigative assistance may assist the Inspector General
provisions.quote: “No officer, employee, agent, contractor, or subcontractor in the judicial branch may discharge, demote, threaten, suspend, harass, or in any other manner discriminate against an employee” … “An employee injured by a violation of subsection (a) may, in a civil action, obtain appropriate relief.”
provisions.context: Proposed §1026 would prohibit a judicial-branch officer, employee, agent, contractor, or subcontractor from taking the listed forms of employment retaliation against an employee because of a lawful act that provides information, causes information to be provided, or otherwise assists an investigation into a possible Federal-law or regulatory violation or misconduct by a judge, justice, or other judicial-branch employee, where the covered activity or investigation may assist the Inspector General in performing duties under the chapter. An injured employee could seek appropriate relief in a civil action. Although contractors and subcontractors appear in the list of potential retaliators, the protected person and civil plaintiff are described as an employee; the text does not define whether that term includes employees of judicial-branch contractors or subcontractors, and it does not expressly protect a contractor or subcontractor in that capacity. It also specifies no confidential disclosure channel, administrative complaint process, specific court, jurisdiction, venue, limitations period, exhaustion rule, burden of proof, attorney-fee rule, or list of available remedies.
goals: Protect employees covered by proposed §1026 from employment retaliation for lawful disclosures or investigative assistance that may assist the Inspector General.
Enable employees covered by proposed §1026 to provide or cause the provision of information about possible legal or regulatory violations or misconduct for use in judicial-branch oversight.
Give an employee injured by prohibited retaliation a civil path to appropriate relief.

effects.text: The provision would make the listed adverse employment actions unlawful when caused by a covered employee's lawful provision of information or assistance. It could reduce fear of reporting, but the text does not guarantee awareness, confidentiality, use of the information, or freedom from retaliation.

Officers, employees, agents, contractors, and subcontractors could be prohibited retaliators, while the person protected and authorized to sue is described only as an employee. The text does not define whether that term includes employees of judicial-branch contractors or subcontractors, and it does not expressly protect a contractor or subcontractor in that capacity.

An injured employee could pursue appropriate relief in a civil action, creating an enforcement route outside the Inspector General's reporting powers. The bill leaves the specific court, jurisdiction, venue, timing, proof rules, exhaustion, fees, and remedy boundaries unstated.

barriers.text: A claimant would have to identify and pursue a civil action and establish the required connection among lawful covered conduct that may assist the Inspector General, possible wrongdoing, an adverse employment action, and resulting injury without statutory procedural detail.

Courts would have to resolve threshold and remedial questions that the bill does not answer, including who qualifies as an employee, what causation standard applies, what procedure governs, and what relief is appropriate.

The text creates a prohibition but no required notice, training, confidential intake channel, administrative adjudication, or compliance-reporting system through which covered workers and potential retaliators would learn or operationalize it.

The bill requires no statistics on protected disclosures, alleged retaliation, civil filings, settlements, judgments, remedies, or employee willingness to report. Raw lawsuit counts would not distinguish more retaliation from greater awareness and access to enforcement.
